books.section: Topic 6.13 Politics in the Gilded Age

primary_sources: Thomas Nast, 'The Brains,' Harper's Weekly, October 21, 1871
Rutherford B. Hayes, inaugural address, March 5, 1877
Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act, January 16, 1883
Grover Cleveland, annual message to Congress, December 6, 1887

prompt: Evaluate the extent to which the major political parties addressed the economic concerns of farmers and workers in the period 1871–1896.

documents.title: Nast on Boss Tweed
documents.source: Thomas Nast, “The Brains,” Harper’s Weekly, October 21, 1871. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A cartoonist attacking the Tammany Hall machine, drawing for a middle-class magazine readership.

documents.title: Hayes on Party and Country
documents.source: Rutherford B. Hayes, inaugural address, March 5, 1877. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A new president speaking after a disputed election, promising to serve the country above his party.
documents.text: “The President of the United States of necessity owes his election to office to the suffrage and zealous labors of a political party, the members of which cherish with ardor and regard as of essential importance the principles of their party organization; but he should strive to be always mindful of the fact that he serves his party best who serves the country best.”

documents.title: The Pendleton Act Creates a Civil Service Commission
documents.source: Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act, January 16, 1883, Section 1. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A federal law written after Garfield's assassination, setting up merit hiring for some federal jobs.
documents.text: “That the President is authorized to appoint, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate, three persons, not more than two of whom shall be adherents of the same party, as Civil Service Commissioners, and said three commissioners shall constitute the United States Civil Service Commission.”

documents.title: Cleveland on the Tariff
documents.source: Grover Cleveland, annual message to Congress, December 6, 1887. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A Democratic president devoting his whole annual message to the tariff, arguing for lower rates.
documents.text: “When we consider that the theory of our institutions guarantees to every citizen the full enjoyment of all the fruits of his industry and enterprise, with only such deduction as may be his share toward the careful and economical maintenance of the Government which protects him, it is plain that the exaction of more than this is indefensible extortion and a culpable betrayal of American fairness and justice.”

documents.title: The Sherman Silver Purchase Act Orders Silver Buying
documents.source: Sherman Silver Purchase Act, July 14, 1890, Section 1. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A federal law passed as a bargain between western silver interests and eastern protectionists.
documents.text: “That the Secretary of the Treasury is hereby directed to purchase, from time to time, silver bullion to the aggregate amount of four million five hundred thousand ounces, or so much thereof as may be offered in each month, at the market price thereof, not exceeding one dollar for three hundred and seventy-one and twenty-five hundredths grains of pure silver, and to issue in payment for such purchases of silver bullion Treasury notes of the United States to be prepared by the Secretary of the Treasury, in such form and of such denominations, not less than one dollar nor more than one thousand dollars, as he may prescribe.”

documents.title: The Omaha Platform Demands Free Silver
documents.source: People’s Party, Omaha Platform, July 4, 1892. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A new third party's founding statement, written to indict the old parties and rally farmers and workers.
documents.text: “We demand free and unlimited coinage of silver and gold at the present legal ratio of 16 to 1.”

documents.title: Presidential Election Results, 1876–1896
documents.source: Presidential election returns, 1876–1896, American Presidency Project. Public data.
documents.sourcing: Official returns compiled after each election, showing how close the contests ran and where a third party broke through.

rubric.criterion: Thesis: earns the point for a historically defensible claim that answers the prompt, stating the extent to which the major parties addressed the economic concerns of farmers and workers between 1871 and 1896, with a clear line of reasoning.
rubric.notEarned: Restating the prompt with no claim about the extent of change does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Contextualization: earns the point for describing a broader historical context relevant to the prompt, such as industrialization building giant corporations and crowded cities, or farmers facing falling prices and railroad rates they could not control.
rubric.notEarned: A sentence of background with no link to the argument does not earn the point.

rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than three documents, or quoting documents without describing what they show, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (second point): earns the point for using the content of at least six documents to support an argument, with the evidence accurately described and tied to the claim.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than six documents, or listing documents without connecting them to the argument, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence beyond the documents: earns the point for describing a specific and relevant example beyond the documents, such as the Interstate Commerce Act of 1887, the Panic of 1893, Coxey's Army of 1894, or the election of 1896.
rubric.notEarned: A general statement with no specific example beyond the documents does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Sourcing: earns the point for explaining the relevance of a document's author, purpose, audience, or historical situation to the argument, for at least two documents.
rubric.notEarned: Identifying an author without explaining why it matters, or sourcing only one document, does not earn the point.

rubric.notEarned: A second example with no qualification or weighing does not earn the point.

modelOutline:
Thesis: Between 1871 and 1896 the major parties addressed farmers' and workers' economic concerns only slightly, offering tariff debate, civil-service reform, and a silver-purchase law while leaving the deeper demands for cheap money, fair railroad rates, and government ownership unmet, so that farmers built a third party of their own.
Context: Industrialization built giant corporations and crowded cities, while farmers faced falling crop prices, heavy debts, and railroad rates they could not control, and the older American suspicion of strong government still shaped how presidents and judges answered new demands.
Evidence: Documents 3 and 5 show the parties responding in part, as the Pendleton Act put some federal jobs under merit rules and the Sherman Silver Purchase Act ordered the Treasury to buy silver each month. Document 4 shows the Democrats answering through the tariff, as Cleveland attacked high rates as extortion.
Evidence continued: Documents 1 and 6 show the demands the parties failed to meet, as Nast's cartoon charges Tweed's machine with ruling by money and the Omaha Platform demands free silver at 16 to 1. Document 2 shows Hayes promising that serving the country serves the party best, a promise the record tests.
Evidence continued: Document 7 shows why the parties finally listened, as Weaver's 22 electoral votes in 1892 proved that farmers could carry states outside the two-party hold, and McKinley's 51 percent in 1896 shows the major parties winning back the country by absorbing the silver issue.
Beyond the documents: The Interstate Commerce Act of 1887 created the first federal railroad regulator after the Wabash decision, and the Panic of 1893 threw millions out of work while Coxey's Army marched on Washington asking for federal jobs, which Cleveland ignored.
Sourcing: Nast draws for a middle-class magazine readership to expose corruption, so his cartoon is an attack, not a neutral report, while the Omaha Platform is a new party's own program, so its demands show what farmers wanted rather than what government did.
Complexity: The parties answered some demands in law while guarding the interests of business, so the same years produced both the first railroad regulator and a tariff that raised farmers' costs, and the Populists gained votes precisely because the answers fell short.
